node.label: Bruce Curtis
node.date_label: With Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation” 1985 · Building the Educational State 1988 · True Government by Choice Men? 1992 · The Politics of Population 2001 · “After ‘Canada’” 2009 · Ruling by Schooling Quebec 2012
node.description: A historical sociologist (Carleton University) whose studies of schooling, school inspection and the census in the Canadas read administration as a means of rule. In Building the Educational State (1988), as a reviewer quotes it, education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (p. 110), and the educational state was built 'only through the destruction of a prior educational organization' (p. 15); in True Government by Choice Men? (1992) 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (p. 32). His census history (2001) holds that 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (p. 305, as Belshaw quotes it), and in a 1996 review he wrote that 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns'. Reviewers credited his joining of Foucault's analysis of power to a Marxist theory of state formation but found gender relations missing (Davey 1989; Miller 1993), and Bryan Palmer judged the inspection study, taken as a model, 'overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (1993). In the debate over Ian McKay's liberal order framework, Nancy Christie cites 'Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality' (2009).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Bruce Curtis (b. 1950); with Philip Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation: A Preliminary Statement” (CHA Historical Papers, 1985); Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (1988); True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (1992); The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (2001); “After ‘Canada’: Liberalisms, Social Theory, and Historical Analysis” (2009); Ruling by Schooling Quebec: Conquest to Liberal Governmentality – A Historical Sociology (2012).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Curtis's state-formation studies of schooling, inspection and the census (1985–2001) and their place in the liberal order debate. Read on 2026-10-14: his review of Darroch and Soltow (1996, pp. 107–110) in full, and four in-period or near-period reviews of his books in full: Davey (1989) on Building the Educational State, Miller (1993) and Palmer (1993) on True Government by Choice Men?, and Belshaw (2002) on The Politics of Population; Christie (2009) was re-read for its Curtis passage. His books are unread: his words from them are reviewers' quotations, with the reviewers' page references. The 1985 article with Corrigan, the 2009 chapter and Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012) are title- or summary-level only. He is a sociologist, not a historian by department; the atlas's moral regulation entry treats his state-formation work as shared ground with the liberal order framework, not membership.

proposed_edges.relationship: Schooling, school inspection and the census studied as state formation in the Canadas: education as 'government of the self' (1988), inspection as the making of 'relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (1992), the census as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001); work that predates the framework, and that Christie later cites for the point that McKay describes governmentality (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period reviews, read in full; Curtis's books are unread, so his words are the reviewers' quotations with their page references. Davey (Historical Studies in Education 1, 1989, pp. 161–165) on Building the Educational State (1988): 'one of the great strengths of Curtis' approach is his grounding of Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity within a marxist theory of state formation and cultural forms' (p. 161); he quotes Curtis that 'the construction of the Educational State was accomplished only through the destruction of a prior educational organization and the marginalization of the structure of educational possibilities' (book p. 15), that schooling meant 'the anchoring of the conditions of political governance in the selves of the governed' (no page given), that education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (book p. 110) and that 'public education was administered into dominance only through a myriad of local struggles' (book p. 132); Davey notes 'there is no reference to Gramsci or the theory of hegemony in the bibliography or the index' (p. 162) and objects that Curtis 'fails to provide an adequate account of patriarchal relations in the period' (p. 165). Miller (Historical Studies in Education 5, 1993, pp. 123–126) on True Government by Choice Men? (1992) quotes 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (book p. 32) and 'Bureaucratic administration was seen by political liberals as practical education, a ‘normal school’ for the people' (book p. 7); she says Curtis 'carefully distances himself' from a social-control argument (p. 124) and regrets 'the relative invisibility of gender relations' (p. 125). Bryan Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, pp. 365–367): 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); yet he credits Curtis and Colonial Leviathan with 'the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366). Later readings: Belshaw (2002, read) quotes the census book: 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305). Christie (Underhill Review 2009, read): 'Here I think we need to be alert to Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality'; this is Christie's characterisation, and Curtis's own 2009 chapter ('After ‘Canada’') is unread. The edge records a contribution to the strand the atlas calls 'State formation before the framework'; the work predates McKay's prospectus (2000, unread beyond its abstract), and no checked text by McKay names Curtis. The collaboration with Philip Corrigan (1985) is title-level; the moral regulation entry treats this state-formation work as shared ground (edge_848), so no separate Curtis edge to moral_regulation is drawn.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: state_formation_roots ('State formation before the framework') holds Curtis, Greer and Radforth and lof_curtis_1988/1992/2001/2012; it is exactly the claim. debate_2009 also holds him, for the 2009 chapter, which is unread.
proposed_edges.roster_row_note: His liberal_order_framework row (historian) describes 'state formation through schooling, inspection and the census' and Christie's governmentality credit: the same intervention.

proposed_edges.relationship: Census returns read as artefacts of state knowledge rather than transparent records: objections to inferring property, gender and inheritance from the 1871 Ontario census in a review of Darroch and Soltow (1996), and census making as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Curtis's 1996 review of Gordon Darroch and Lee Soltow's census study of property in Ontario (1994) and his census history (2001); it is not a verdict on quantitative history as a whole, and Darroch and Soltow are not in the atlas. His own words (Historical Studies in Education 8, 1996, pp. 107–110, read in full): 'Anyone who has worked with manuscript census data must be impressed with the meticulous and painstaking analysis undertaken here' (p. 109); 'Two related critical points seem worth making about census artifacts and the matter of gender' (p. 109); the authors 'go so far as to suggest that their cross-sectional study is actually longitudinal' (p. 109); 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns, although, as an ideological practice, census-taking attached property to adult men' (pp. 109–110); and, qualifying, 'the book is an important contribution to ongoing debates' (p. 110). The census book (2001) is unread; as Belshaw quotes it (2002, read), 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305), and it 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26). Belshaw's reading, in his words: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout', and 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'. Kind: critique, because the 1996 text objects to inferences drawn from census returns; it is not a rejection of quantitative work, and Curtis calls the book he reviews an important contribution.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No quant strand covers census-based social history of Canada. The nearest is quant/colonial_labour_categories (Kumar on changing census categories), a different case; demography (aggregate_population) was considered and is less apt, since the reviewed book is a property study, not a population reconstruction.

new_sources.title: Ian Davey, review of Bruce Curtis, Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (1988), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 1, no. 1 (1989): 161–165.
new_sources.citation: Ian Davey, review of Bruce Curtis, Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (Lewes and London, ON: Falmer Press and Althouse Press, 1988), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 1, no. 1 (1989): 161–165.

verification.note: Read in full from the journal's own PDF (galley 1498; scanned, local English OCR; folios 162–165 from the running heads, the first page being 161 per the OJS record). Passages used: Corrigan's preface, Curtis 'makes us see differently' (p. 9 of the book, as Davey quotes it; the OCR reads 'dif3ferently'); 'one of the great strengths of Curtis' approach is his grounding of Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity within a marxist theory of state formation and cultural forms' (p. 161); Curtis's argument that 'the construction of the Educational State was accomplished only through the destruction of a prior educational organization and the marginalization of the structure of educational possibilities' (book p. 15, quoted pp. 161–162); 'there is no reference to Gramsci or the theory of hegemony in the bibliography or the index' (p. 162); state schooling as 'the anchoring of the conditions of political governance in the selves of the governed' (no page given by Davey; p. 162); education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (book p. 110, quoted p. 163); 'public education was administered into dominance only through a myriad of local struggles' (book p. 132, quoted p. 163); 'My major criticism of Curtis is that he fails to provide an adequate account of patriarchal relations in the period', his framework 'privileges class conflicts' (p. 165).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period review of Building the Educational State; the main witness to the book's wording.

new_sources.citation: Pavla Miller, review of Bruce Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education and State Formation in Canada West (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 5, no. 1 (1993): 123–126.

verification.note: Read in full from the journal's own PDF (galley 1145; scanned, local English OCR; folios 123–126). Passages used: Curtis 'makes a significant contribution to history and sociology by utilizing some key insights from the work of Foucault and other theorists, but takes exemplary care with historical evidence' (p. 123); 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (book p. 32, quoted p. 123); 'no central state agency could govern a population about which it was ignorant' (book p. 30, quoted pp. 123–124); 'Bureaucratic administration was seen by political liberals as practical education, a ‘normal school’ for the people' (book p. 7, quoted p. 124); 'Such concerns suggest a social control problematic, and Curtis carefully distances himself from this form of argument', depicting 'an ever-contested and incomplete process of rule' (p. 124); 'My major problem with this excellent book concerns the relative invisibility of gender relations' (p. 125).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period review of the inspection study.

new_sources.title: Bryan D. Palmer, review of Bruce Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? (1992), and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992), Labour/Le Travail 31 (1993): 365–367.
new_sources.citation: Bryan D. Palmer, joint review of Bruce Curtis, True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992) and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth Century Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992), Labour/Le Travail 31 (1993): 365–367 (in the issue's 'Reviews / Comptes Rendus' section, pp. 365–433).

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 365–367) in the journal's own PDF of the reviews section (lltjournal.ca article 4891, galley 5764; scanned pages with a text layer; folios 365, 366 and 367 printed in the running heads). Passages used: 'THESE BOOKS are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada'; 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); Curtis 'telescopes the process of state formation in Canada West in the 1840s into the emergence of educational inspectors' and 'this study is too minutely focused' (p. 365); the promotional claim that Curtis 'presents a systematic application of the insights of ... Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Gramsci, and Foucault' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); 'the collection lacks coherence' (p. 366); 'The single most important contribution of the articles in this collection, also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); the gender essays read as 'complementary to the revisionist assessment of ‘responsible government’ as an expression of a slight [sic] of hand that promised popular sovereignty at the same time as it delivered institutionalized subordination and regulation' (pp. 366–367); 'Books like these make the job easier' (p. 367). Palmer names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (the text layer prints the name as 'Allan Green's', p. 366).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period critique of Curtis's inspection study and of Colonial Leviathan, by the atlas's Bryan Palmer. Used in the Curtis and Greer entries.

new_sources.title: John Douglas Belshaw, review of Bruce Curtis, The Politics of Population (2001), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 14, no. 1 (2002): 122–125.
new_sources.citation: John Douglas Belshaw, review of Bruce Curtis, The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2001), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 14, no. 1 (2002): review section pp. 121–185.

verification.note: Read in full from the journal's own PDF (galley 2025; text layer). The running heads give pp. 123–125 for the second to fourth pages, so the review runs pp. 122–125; the OJS record gives first page 121 and last page 124. Review pages are therefore not used as locators; quotations of the book carry Belshaw's references to the book. Passages used: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout'; 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305); census making 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26); 'a uniform enumeration would make a single Canadian population when in fact there were two' (book p. 98); 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'; criticisms: the Nova Scotian and New Brunswick systems grafted on 'as though they were unproblematic', no bibliography, and 'deadening jargon' in the introduction and conclusion.

new_sources.scope_note: Near-period (2002) review; the witness to the census book's wording.

row.context: Historical sociologist of the census who treats census returns as artefacts of state knowledge: reviewing Darroch and Soltow's study of the 1871 Ontario census (1996) he wrote that 'The census simply cannot tell us much' about how property was valued, gendered or inherited, while calling the book 'an important contribution'; his census history (2001) calls census making 'the making of things to be taken' (as Belshaw quotes it).
